system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mrs. ___ was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and transient low-grade fever. Workup including CT scans of the head, abdomen, and pelvis, as well as cardiac enzymes, showed no acute pathology. Her symptoms were attributed to viral gastroenteritis, and she was treated with IV fluids and Zofran with good response. A mildly abnormal urinalysis prompted a course of ciprofloxacin despite negative cultures. Her chronic conditions—including hypertension, neuropathic chest pain, rheumatoid arthritis, and narcotic-treated pain—were managed with her baseline medications. She improved clinically, tolerated oral intake, and was discharged home with follow-up arranged. Her narcotic contract was continued, and she was advised to maintain laxative use.
problems: Intestinal infection due to other organism, not elsewhere classified
Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of breast
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of bronchus and lung

FINDINGS:  The cardiac silhouette appears normal in size and unchanged from
___.  There is a rightward shift of the mediastinum with
elevated right hemidiaphragm, consistent with right lung volume loss. 
Surgical material is noted within the right hilus, consistent with remote
right upper lobectomy.  The pulmonary vasculature appears unremarkable.  The
bilateral lungs appear well aerated, with no evidence of consolidation or
pleural effusion.

The visualized osseous structures show no evidence of gross skeletal
abnormalities.

IMPRESSION:  No acute cardiopulmonary process.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mrs. ___. I’m Dr. ___. You came in today because of shortness of breath and chest pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve been having trouble breathing for a few days now. I’ve been using my nebulizer more often—three times a day—and my inhaler every few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned a cough with yellow sputum. Any fever or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever, but I’ve been feeling cold lately. I’ve had chills off and on. The chest pain started two days ago while I was sitting—doesn’t get worse when I walk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And any swelling in your legs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my feet have been swollen since mid-week. I’ve been using Lasix at home when it gets bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We’ll check your lungs and heart. Given your history of asthma and lung cancer, we want to make sure this isn’t pneumonia or a heart issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried it might be fluid in my lungs. Or maybe my asthma flaring up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good concern. We’ve ordered a chest X-ray to check for that. We also did blood work and a troponin to rule out heart strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I’ve had asthma for years, but this feels a bit worse than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your chest X-ray came back. Good news—no signs of pneumonia or fluid in the lungs. Your heart size is normal, and there’s no acute issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So what’s causing the shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like an asthma exacerbation. The wheezing we heard, plus your increased use of inhalers, supports that. The yellow sputum and chills make us think there might be a mild infection triggering it, so we’ll treat with antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So it’s not my lung cancer coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s nothing on the X-ray to suggest that. The changes we see are from your past lobectomy—right side looks smaller, which is expected. No new masses or collapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That really worries me, so I’m glad to hear that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’ll start you on a short course of prednisone to reduce airway inflammation and azithromycin for five days to cover any infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve taken prednisone before—it helps, but I don’t sleep well on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it can affect sleep. We’re using a rapid taper—40mg for three days, then 20mg for three—so side effects should be minimal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Advair and nebulizers—I should keep using them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. We’ll also give you albuterol nebs every four hours as needed. Your home regimen stays the same otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, I think. I used the nebulizer only twice last night. Breathing feels easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. Your oxygen levels are stable at 97% on room air. We’ll keep you on the antibiotics and steroids, and continue monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My daughter asked if I should start using the nicotine patch. I’ve been trying to quit smoking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s an excellent idea. We can start you on a 7mg patch—use half daily to reduce withdrawal. It’s important for your lung health, especially with asthma and your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it. I’ve been cutting back, but it’s hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your labs. Your white count is normal, troponin is negative—no sign of infection or heart strain. All good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure? It’s usually high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s been elevated—176 over 98 on admission—but we’re continuing your home meds: lisinopril, metoprolol, and valsartan. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take those every day. And my pain meds—morphine and Roxicet—are still okay to use?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing your chronic pain regimen. Your joint and back pain are well managed. No new issues there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your breathing has improved significantly. We’d like to discharge you today if you’re feeling up to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the prednisone taper as prescribed—40mg for three days, then 20mg for three. Take azithromycin for two more days. Use albuterol nebs every four hours if short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the inhalers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back to your regular Advair and Singulair. Continue as before. Also, keep using the nicotine patch—half a patch daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Lasix for swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, take it as needed for swelling, and remember to take your potassium on those days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I think I’ve got it. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll send all instructions and prescriptions to your pharmacy. Follow up with your primary doctor in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my breathing gets worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your rescue inhaler or nebulizer. If no improvement in 20 minutes, or if you feel worse, go to the ER or call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. Keep up the good work with quitting smoking and managing your asthma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mrs. ___ was admitted for shortness of breath, left-sided chest pain, and bilateral foot swelling. She had increased use of albuterol and nebulizers at home, with a cough producing yellow sputum and subjective chills. Evaluation revealed no acute cardiopulmonary process on chest X-ray, normal troponin, and stable labs. Her symptoms were attributed to an acute asthma exacerbation, possibly triggered by a mild respiratory infection. She was treated with a six-day prednisone taper, a five-day course of azithromycin, and continued bronchodilator therapy. Her chronic conditions, including hypertension, rheumatoid arthritis, and chronic pain, were managed with baseline medications. She improved clinically, maintained oxygen saturation on room air, and was discharged home with instructions to complete her medications, continue home inhalers, and start a nicotine patch to aid smoking cessation. Follow-up was arranged with her primary care provider.
